parts.problem_md: Explain **one **advantage to a business of selling in international markets.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage of selling in international markets is that a business can reach a much larger number of potential customers **[1]**. Selling only in a domestic market limits the size of the audience a business can target **[1]**; expanding into international markets opens up opportunities to sell to millions more consumers in other countries, increasing total sales and revenue **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Selling in international markets means targeting customers in other countries, beyond the domestic market
> - Advantages of international markets include
> 
>   - Access to more customers
>   - Potential for economies of scale
>   - Risk spreading
>   - Exposure to new ideas
>   - Avoiding a saturated domestic market
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Access to a larger number of potential customers increases total sales and revenue, which can lead to higher profit for the business
> - Selling greater volumes across international markets allows a business to produce on a larger scale, reducing the average cost per unit through economies of scale, which improves profit margins
> - Operating in several countries spreads risk - if demand falls in one market, sales in other countries can help compensate, making the business more financially stable
> - International markets may be growing faster than the domestic market, allowing a business to increase revenue without having to compete harder at home where the market may already be saturated
> - Exposure to different customer preferences in other countries can generate new product ideas and help the business innovate, keeping it competitive
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]** > **Benjamin’s Beds (BB) ** > > Benjamin’s Beds (BB) is a large manufacturer of beds and has a strong brand image for quality. Its main channel of distribution is through the producer market (B2B) to national hotel chains. Recently, BB has also entered the consumer market (B2C) by selling online direct to customers. > > BB uses flow production. BB’s existing machinery is old and cannot satisfy the increased demand. The directors of BB have decided its existing machinery needs replacing. Table 2.1 shows data for existing and proposed new machinery. > > **Table 2.1 Data for existing and proposed new machinery** > > | | Variable cost per unit
(\$) | Output per year | > |---|---|---| > | Existing machinery | 50 | 5000 | > | New machinery | 40 | 7500 | > > Fixed costs are \$500 000 per year. Using new machinery would reduce this by 10%. > > BB sales data suggests that its market share is growing rapidly. The consumer market (B2C) is becoming more important to BB because online orders are increasing. However, online demand is for a wide range of bed styles. The consumer market requires a substantial marketing budget and some retraining of employees. > > Orders from national hotel chains in the producer market (B2B) are for a more limited range of bed styles. These orders remain constant with low marketing costs. However, BB is increasingly under pressure to reduce prices to hotels. > > BB uses non-financial motivators and until recently had a motivated workforce. Efficiency is falling due to employees having to work longer hours because of increased demand. This is decreasing staff morale and welfare. Recommend whether BB should focus on the producer market (B2B) or the consumer market (B2C). Justify your recommendation.
parts.solution_md:
BB could focus on the consumer market **[K]**. Online orders are increasing and BB's market share is growing rapidly **[Ap]**, and its strong brand image for quality matters far more to individual consumers than to hotel buyers, who are pressing BB to reduce its prices **[An]**. Selling direct also removes the bargaining power of the national chains, so BB would keep more of the value it adds instead of surrendering it in price negotiations **[An]**. However, consumer demand is for a wide range of bed styles, which sits badly with flow production, and BB would need a substantial marketing budget and staff retraining at a time when efficiency and morale are already falling **[E]**

BB could instead focus on the producer market **[K]**. Orders from hotel chains are for a limited range of styles and remain constant, which is exactly what flow production needs **[Ap]**. Running the new machinery at its full 7500 beds would cut total cost per bed from \$150 to \$100, because the same \$750 000 of total cost is spread across 50% more output **[An]**. That \$50 saving on every bed is what would allow BB to absorb the hotels' pressure on price and still widen its margin **[An]**. However, constant orders mean no growth, and depending on a few national chains that are already pushing prices down leaves BB badly exposed if one of them goes elsewhere **[E]**

I recommend that BB focus on the producer market **[E]**. The decisive point is that BB has just committed to new flow production machinery, and flow production delivers its cost advantage only when it runs long, uninterrupted batches of a limited range **[E]**. Chasing the variety the online market wants would mean frequent changeovers, so BB would never reach the 7500 beds on which the fall to \$100 depends, and would have paid for capacity it could not use **[Ap]**. The workforce position points the same way, since efficiency and morale are already falling and the consumer market would add retraining and marketing demands on top **[E]**. BB should not abandon B2C, which is growing and suits its brand, but should keep it as a secondary channel offering a deliberately narrow range of styles until the new machinery is running efficiently and the pressure on staff has eased **[E]**

> **[case-study]**
> **Clever Televisions (CTV) **
> 
> CTV is a public limited company that produces and sells televisions. It has been operating in country A for 30 years. CTV owns 3 factories and has over 100 employees. CTV’s factories use a combination of capital and skilled labour to produce the televisions. The leadership style in all the factories is autocratic. Employees’ pay is based on time worked each week.
> 
> The CTV brand is known for high‑quality and reliability. It targets high‑income customers. CTV uses price skimming when it launches a new product.
> 
> In total, 6 million televisions were sold in country A in 2019. Table 2.1 shows market growth data.
> 
> **Table 2.1: Television sales in country A**
> 
> | **Year** | **Market growth** |
> |---|---|
> | 2020 | +2% |
> | 2021 | +1% |
> | 2022 | –3% (forecast) |
> 
> The market for televisions in country A is very competitive and the business environment is dynamic. CTV plans to introduce a lower priced television brand to appeal to the mass market. This brand will be known as STV.
> 
> CTV has decided to introduce automation into one of its factories to produce the STV televisions. This will lead to redundancies in that factory.
> 
> The employees in the other two factories are concerned they might also face redundancy and so motivation is currently low. The Human Resources Director recommends that CTV should find ways in which employees can participate in the management and control of the business.

Calculate the total number of televisions sold in country A in 2021.
parts.solution_md:
**6.1812 million**** [3]**

$\frac{\mathrm{Previous} \mathrm{sales}--\mathrm{current} \mathrm{sales}}{\mathrm{Previous} \mathrm{sales}}\times100$     **[1]**

$2020\mathrm{sales}=6\mathrm{million}\times1.02=6.12\mathrm{million}\,\,2021\mathrm{sales}=6.12\mathrm{million}\times1.01=6.1812\mathrm{million}$     **[2]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Up to 2 marks for valid workings
> - 1 mark for the correct answer of 6.1812 million
> 
> A correct answer with no working shown still receives full marks.

parts.problem_md: Define the term ‘national market’.
parts.solution_md:
A national market is a market where a business operates and sells its products only within its own country **[1]**, rather than trading overseas **[1]**

> - A business with branches and operations within one country

parts.problem_md: Evaluate the importance of market share to a business operating in a competitive retail market.
parts.solution_md:
One reason market share is important in a competitive retail market is that a higher share often allows the business to benefit from economies of scale **[K]**. As a business sells more units, it can buy in larger quantities and negotiate lower prices from suppliers than smaller competitors can. Lower costs allow the business to either reduce its prices to attract more customers, or maintain prices and earn higher profit margins **[An]**. In a competitive retail market where customers are sensitive to price **[Ap]**, this cost advantage can be decisive - a business with a large market share is better placed to undercut rivals and win sales **[An]**

Market share also reflects the relative strength of a business against its competitors **[K]**. A large market share usually means the business is well-known to customers, making it the first choice when they decide where to shop **[Ap]**. This brand recognition makes it easier to retain loyal customers without spending heavily on marketing **[An]**. However, the importance of market share is not the same for every retail business. A niche retailer - for example, one selling premium organic food **[Ap]** - may have a small market share but still be highly profitable, because its customers are willing to pay higher prices and are less likely to switch to cheaper alternatives **[An]**

Overall, market share is an important measure for most businesses in a competitive retail market **[E]**, but its significance depends on the business's objectives and the nature of the market. For a large retailer competing on price - such as a supermarket **[Ap]** - a high market share is crucial because it underpins the cost advantages that allow the business to stay competitive. For a smaller niche retailer, profitability and customer loyalty may matter more **[E]**. In highly competitive retail markets, gaining market share is likely to be closely linked to long-term success, but it should be seen as a means to an end rather than an objective in itself **[E]**

> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two reasons why market share is important to a business operating in a competitive retail market. |
> | **1** | - Shows understanding of one reason why market share is important to a business operating in a competitive retail market. |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |

> | **2** | - Analysis based on two reasons why market share is important to a business operating in a competitive retail market. |

> 
> **Indicative content **
> 
> - Market share is the sales of one business as a proportion of total sales across the whole market, usually expressed as a percentage
> - A retail business with a large market share can claim to be the brand leader in its market
> 
>   - It can use this status in its advertising - for example, promoting itself as "the UK's number one" - which reinforces its reputation with customers and makes it harder for competitors to win them away
>   - In a competitive retail market where many businesses sell similar products, brand leader status can be a significant advantage in attracting and keeping customers
> - In some retail markets dominated by a small number of large businesses, the firm with the greatest market share may be able to influence the prices charged across the market
> 
>   - If competitors are smaller, they may be forced to match the price leader's decisions
>   - This gives the market leader greater control over its revenue and profit margins, which smaller rivals do not have
> - Whether market share matters depends partly on the size and growth rate of the total market
> 
>   - If the total retail market is growing rapidly - for example, due to rising consumer incomes or changing shopping habits - even a business with a small market share may be achieving strong growth in its actual sales
>   - In this case, the rate of market growth may matter more to the business than its share of the market
> - The importance of market share also depends on a business's objectives
> 
>   - A retail business that aims to maximise profit in a specific niche - for example, selling premium goods to a small, loyal customer base - may not need a large overall market share to achieve its goals
>   - Profitability matters more to such a business than market dominance
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.solution_md:

parts.problem_md: Analyse **two **possible benefits to a business of increasing its market share.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit of increasing market share is that it allows a business to benefit from economies of scale **[K]**. As a business sells more products and grows its share of the market, it can produce in larger quantities. This spreads fixed costs, such as factory rent and management salaries, across more units, reducing the cost of producing each one **[An]**. Lower unit costs gives a retail business, for example, two options - it can reduce its prices to attract even more customers and win further market share, or it can keep prices the same and earn a higher profit on each sale **[Ap]**. Either way, growing market share through economies of scale strengthens the business's competitive position **[An]** A second benefit is increased brand recognition **[K]**. As a business increases its share of the market, more consumers become familiar with its name and products. A well-known brand builds trust with customers, making them more likely to choose it over less familiar competitors without needing to be convinced by large amounts of advertising **[An]**. This customer loyalty means the business can rely on repeat purchases, which makes its revenue more stable and reduces the cost of constantly finding new customers **[An]**. For a business which already holds a high market share, further growth would make its brand even more recognisable, making it harder for competitors to win customers away **[Ap]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md: Explain the link between corporate objectives and marketing objectives of a business.
parts.solution_md:
Marketing objectives are set to help a business achieve its corporate objectives **[1]**. Corporate objectives are broad, business-wide goals that cannot be achieved by one department alone - they must be broken down into smaller, specific targets for each department **[1]**. The marketing department's targets are designed to contribute directly to the overall goal **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Corporate objectives are the overall goals of the whole business, such as survival, profit maximisation, or revenue growth — they set the direction for every department
> - Marketing objectives are the specific targets set for the marketing department, such as increasing market share, building brand awareness, boosting sales, or developing customer loyalty
> - Both types of objective are usually expressed in measurable, time-bound terms (e.g. increase market share by 5% within two years)
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Marketing objectives are derived from corporate objectives — they break the overall business goal down into specific targets that the marketing function is responsible for delivering
> - Corporate and marketing objectives must be aligned; if they point in different directions, the marketing department's activities will not help the business achieve its overall goals
> - Without marketing objectives that support the corporate objectives, the marketing budget may be spent on activities that do not contribute to what the business is ultimately trying to achieve
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
'The setting of effective marketing objectives is the most important factor for the successful launch of a new women’s football (soccer) team.'

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
Marketing objectives are the specific targets a business sets for its marketing activities **[K]**. For a new women's football team, these might include selling a set number of season tickets in the first year or securing a local business sponsor **[Ap]**. Clear objectives give the team direction, helping managers focus resources on the most effective activities and measure progress. For example, if the objective is to attract families, the team can focus on affordable pricing and child-friendly events at the ground **[An]** However, other factors may be more important. Having enough financial resources is critical to any launch **[K]**. Starting a new women's football team requires significant investment - player wages, a ground, kit and marketing costs all need to be paid for **[Ap]**. Without sufficient funding, even well-written marketing objectives cannot be acted upon. Financial backing from investors, sponsors, or local authorities is therefore an essential foundation before any launch strategy can be put into practice **[An]** The quality of the team itself **[K] **also matters greatly. Marketing can attract first-time fans to a match, but if the standard of football is poor, those fans will not return **[Ap]**. Word of mouth is powerful - if early supporters are unimpressed, it will be very difficult to grow a fanbase regardless of how well-targeted the marketing is. The product on the pitch has a major influence on long-term success **[An]** Overall, while effective marketing objectives are an important part of a successful launch, they are not the most important factor **[E]**. Financial resources are likely to matter more, because they are a prerequisite for everything else - without funding, the team cannot recruit quality players, secure a venue, or implement any marketing strategy at all **[An]**. Marketing objectives are only useful if they can actually be put into action **[E]**. A team with strong financial backing and talented players but less precise marketing objectives is more likely to succeed than a team with perfect marketing objectives but insufficient funds. That said, the most successful launch would combine all of these factors - strong finances, a quality team, and well-defined marketing objectives that guide how the team attracts and communicates with supporters **[E]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation > - A full-mark answer will include > > - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout > - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning > - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning > - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed > > **Knowledge and application** > > | **Mark** | **Descriptor** | > |---|---| > | **5** | - Developed knowledge of relevant key term(s) and/or factor(s) is used to answer the question

parts.problem_md: Analyse **two **benefits to a business of niche marketing.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit of niche marketing is that there are fewer competitors **[K]**. In a mass market, many businesses compete for the same large group of customers, making it very hard for any one business to stand out. In a niche market, the customer group is smaller and more specific, so fewer businesses target it. This means a business operating in a niche faces less competition and can build a loyal base of customers more easily **[An]**. For a small business, focusing on a niche, such as being the only local restaurant that sells Asian food with a delivery service **[Ap]**, could attract a dedicated group of customers who have no other option that fully meets their needs **[An]** A second benefit is the ability to charge a higher price **[K]**. Niche products are designed to meet very specific needs, and customers who have those needs are usually willing to pay more for a product that suits them well rather than accepting a cheaper but less suitable alternative. This means a niche business can often earn a higher profit margin on each sale than a business competing in a mass market **[An]**. For example, if a restaurant became the only provider of Asian food with delivery in its area **[Ap]**, it could charge a premium price because customers who want that specific combination have nowhere else to go. parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Barbecue House (BH) **
> 
> BH is a fast food restaurant and takeaway business, which sells a range of burgers, kebabs, pizzas and side orders. BH also has a delivery service to the local area.
> 
> BH is owned by Amir who mortgaged his home to finance the start-up of the business. Amir operates BH as a sole trader. His son also works within the business as a chef. Amir has been advised to change the legal structure of BH and to become a private limited company to protect the business and himself.
> 
> BH is located on a busy high street. There are many other similar businesses on the high street and in the surrounding area. Amir knows that the continued success of the business requires him to identify a gap in the market and develop a unique selling point (USP). Amir has carried out some market research (see Table 1.1 and Fig. 1.1).
> 
> **Table 1.1: Market research data about competitors within 2 km of BH**
> 
> | Total number of competitors | 8 |
> |---|---|
> | Number of competitors who offer delivery services | 4 |
> | Number of competitors who do not sell Asian food | 6 |
> 
> ![Pie chart showing market share: Wok's 20%, Chao’s 20%, Papa Joe’s 10%, Mama Mia's 10%, Pepe’s 10%, Pizza House 5%, Grosetto 5%, TJ’s 5%, BH 15%. Total is $600,000.](assets/001-pie-chart-showing-market-share-wok-s-20-chao-s-2.png)
> 
> **Fig. 1.1: Market share data for competitors within 2 km of BH**
> 
> The two market leaders are Wok’s and Chao’s. Both businesses specialise in Asian food but neither has a delivery service. Amir would like to increase BH’s market share. He is considering starting to sell Asian food. None of his employees have any experience cooking or selling Asian food but Amir believes that the possible increase in income would be worth any extra costs.

Calculate the value in dollars of BH’s share of the market.
parts.solution_md:
**\$90,000 ****[3]**

$BH ' \mathrm{s} \text{market} \text{share} = 100 - Total \text{market} \text{share} of \text{competitors} = 100 - 85 \% = 15 \%$     **[1]**

`Market share value = % market share x Total market value = 15 % x $ 600 , 000 = $ 90 , 000`      **[2]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Up to 2 marks for valid workings
> - 1 mark for the correct answer of £90,000
> 
> A correct answer with no working shown still receives full marks.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **George’s Gym (GG) **
> 
> George identified a potential niche market for a new gym in his local area. He set up GG as a sole trader business three years ago. GG is a modern gym with the latest equipment.
> 
> George has recently gained planning permission to build a new swimming pool. George wants to open the swimming pool because a national competitor is planning to open a new gym close by and he wants GG to remain competitive. The swimming pool will cost \$400 000 and George has yet to decide on the best source of fi nance. He has \$50 000 in savings that he could use and he does not have any mortgage or loans. George is thinking about seeking a private investor but is unsure of the risks involved.
> 
> The local population is wealthy. Last year (2012), GG had 300 members who each paid a membership fee of \$60 per month. George is thinking about new ways of increasing revenue such as offering additional ‘keep fit’ classes. He also plans to increase the monthly fee he charges members to \$66. His accountant has told him he needs to think about the price elasticity of demand before making a pricing decision.
> 
> **Table 3 – Annual revenue and profit for the year for the previous 3 years (\$000)**
> 
> |   | 2010 | 2011 | 2012 |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Annual revenue | 120 | 160 | X |
> | Profit for the year | 20 | 50 | 80 |
> 
> George hopes that the information in Table 3 will help show any potential lender how attractive the gym is as an investment.
> 
> GG has a problem of a high labour turnover of personal trainers. Three of them have left in the last six months. He has just employed a new personal trainer, Sally. George needs to issue her contract of employment. George thinks that the reasons for the high labour turnover include:
> 
> - George is always busy and so he can never offer an effective induction training programme for his employees
> - GG salaries are below average for the industry.

Define the term ‘niche market’.
parts.solution_md:
A small, specific part of a larger market **[1]** in which customers have particular needs or preferences that are not met by mainstream products **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A specialised sector of the market desiring specific products/services
> - Tends to be a very specific target market, such as the wealthy
> - Examples include luxury cars, gluten-free food

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Charlie’s Chocolates (CC) **
> 
> CC is a large public limited company that manufactures a wide range of chocolate bars. Production takes place in low wage countries so that costs can be kept low. CC has suffered recently from poor publicity due to the high levels of sugar used in the production of its chocolate. A national newspaper has recently published an article about how CC exploits employees in low wage countries. The Marketing Director, Alan, is aware of recent trends showing that consumers are becoming more ethical in their buying decisions. He thinks this might explain why sales decreased by 10% last year.
> 
> He has asked to meet with the Managing Director, Ikram, to discuss a major change towards more ethical production methods. This could mean re-locating production back to the home country. This will increase costs and involve the recruitment of additional employees. In response to recent Government guidelines to improve health, Alan wants to decrease the amount of sugar used in the chocolate bars.
> 
> Alan is also thinking about the financial accounts for this year that he received this morning from Ikram (see Table 1 and Table 2).
> 
> **Table 1 – Extract from Income Statement**
> 
> |   | \$000s |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue | 7000 |
> | Cost of sales | 4150 |
> | Gross profit | 2850 |
> | Profit for the year | 1350 |
> | Retained earnings | 565 |
> 
> **Table 2 – Extract from Statement of Financial Position**
> 
> |   | \$000s |
> |---|---|
> | Non-current assets | 3000 |
> | Current assets | 900 |
> | Current liabilities | 400 |
> | Working capital | 500 |
> | Net assets | 3500 |
> 
> With sales declining from last year, Alan has to think carefully about the next steps for marketing. He knows that the product range is of good quality – the problem is the poor image of the company. For example, he is aware that a local consumer group is trying to organise a demonstration outside one of CC’s factories in the next few weeks.

Explain the term ‘marketing’.
parts.solution_md:
Marketing is the process of identifying and satisfying customer needs, using decisions about product, price, place, and promotion to help a business achieve its objectives such as increasing sales **[1]**

For CC, marketing is especially important right now because sales fell by 10% last year, possibly linked to CC's poor public image **[1]**. Effective marketing would involve changing what CC offers - for example, reducing sugar content - and communicating these changes clearly to customers to rebuild trust and bring sales back up **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Marketing is the process of identifying and satisfying customer needs in order to help a business achieve its objectives, such as increasing sales or profit
> - Marketing involves making decisions about the key elements of the marketing mix - product, price, place, and promotion - to ensure the right product reaches the right customer at the right price
> 
> AO2
> 
> - For CC, marketing includes managing the promotion of its chocolate bars to improve the company's image; with sales falling by 10% and consumers becoming more ethical in their buying decisions, CC's marketing must address the negative publicity about high sugar content and the treatment of workers in low-wage countries
> - Effective marketing at CC would also involve decisions about price - which may need to rise if production moves back to the home country - and promotion, to communicate the changes CC is making to a more ethically-minded consumer base
> 
> Accept any other valid response,
